vignette:
At 77, she still carries herself with the crisp, deliberate steadiness of a surgeon, though the steadiness now feels practiced rather than effortless. She is divorced, from Oceania, and has spent most of her adult life in operating rooms where she learned to move quickly, make decisions under pressure, and keep her face composed when others were frightened. That habit of control is part of what makes her story difficult to tell, because even now she speaks of the event as if she is describing a complication in someone else’s chart, though her body remembers it as her own.

The trauma begins with a life-threatening illness that arrives without ceremony. She is healthy enough, busy enough, still working, and then one day the ordinary routine of her life is interrupted by symptoms that feel vaguely off and easy to dismiss. She does what she has always done in medicine: she rationalizes, delays, and tells herself she can finish the week before dealing with it. But the tests come back, the tone of the conversations changes, and suddenly she is no longer the doctor standing at the foot of the bed. She is the patient on the bed, looking up at unfamiliar faces and trying to interpret expressions that reveal more than the words do.

What unsettles her most is not only the fear of dying, but the humiliation of dependency. She is used to being the one who explains risks, who steadies families, who gives difficult news with a calm voice. Now she is the one waiting for someone to return with results, the one trying to read oxygen numbers and scan reports, the one who feels her professional identity begin to fray. She says that during those early days she kept thinking, “This is what other people feel,” as though the realization itself were a shock. She notices the small indignities: needing help to walk, being asked to rest, hearing her own body described in clinical language that feels both intimate and foreign.

The illness becomes life-threatening in a way that turns the world narrow. There are emergency calls, frightening consultations, and moments when she understands, with a kind of cold clarity, that she may not survive. She describes lying awake at night listening for changes in the hallway, certain that each footstep might bring bad news. Her mind starts to race in the dark. She rehearses possible outcomes, bargains silently, and counts the hours until morning. She has flashes of memory from the hospital room that return without warning: the smell of antiseptic, the sound of monitors, the sensation of helplessness in her limbs. Even after the immediate crisis passes, those images do not stay in the past where she wants them to be.

Since then, she lives with a version of vigilance that never fully switches off. She startles at sudden noises, especially the sharp ring of a telephone or alarms in public places, and she feels her chest tighten before she can tell herself she is safe. Medical settings, once familiar and absorbing, now carry a charge she cannot quite explain to others. Walking into a clinic, she becomes aware of every disinfectant smell and every pause in a clinician’s voice. She reads the room before she reads the paperwork. When a doctor enters a bit late, she feels irritation, then fear, then shame for how quickly her mind goes to the worst outcome.

Her days are organized around managing what she can control. She keeps lists. She checks and rechecks appointments. She maintains the routines of a surgeon who has spent decades believing preparation can hold chaos at bay. Yet she finds herself avoiding the very things that would reassure her. She delays reading certain test results, avoids television coverage of hospitals or illness, and turns away from conversations about mortality. At night, the memories are more likely to come. She lies in bed and feels the old panic rising, sometimes with a sense that her body is back in that room before her mind can stop it. On those nights she gets up, makes tea, and sits in the kitchen until the feeling eases.

In quieter moments she grieves the change in herself. She notices that she is less patient than she used to be, more easily exhausted, more easily overwhelmed by uncertainty. She misses the version of her that could enter a crisis and remain cool. At the same time, she is aware of a new vulnerability she cannot dismiss. The illness has made her more cautious, more protective of time, and more aware of how quickly the body can become a place of danger. She continues to work in the profession that once gave her authority, but now she carries into it a private knowledge of what it means to be frightened, helpless, and exposed in a hospital bed.
